notes.2: In this question the most common error was to choose option A, as many candidates read the distance-time graphs as speed-time graphs.
notes.3: Weaker candidates often chose option D here, believing that the acceleration of the stone, rather than its speed, would increase from zero as it fell.
notes.5: Here a number of candidates believed that the force on an object moving in a circle at constant speed would act in its direction of motion.
notes.6: This question was answered correctly by stronger students, with option B being slightly more popular than the correct answer C. This incorrect value is produced by multiplying each force by the distance shown immediately to its left on the diagram; students choosing this did not appreciate that the total distance to the pivot should be used in each case.
notes.8: Incorrect option D was a popular choice with many candidates who did not realise that the momentum does change because its direction changes.
notes.9: A significant proportion of candidates believed that hydroelectric energy is not derived from the Sun.
notes.11: Students should be advised to read questions carefully; many failed to take into account here that there were three boxes.
notes.13: This question concerned a barometer, and a significant number of candidates thought that the space above the column of mercury would increase in length and selected option A.
notes.15: Almost all candidates knew that the average speed of the molecules would increase, but many of them also believed that the average separation would increase, even though the volume of the container was constant.
notes.16: A common error, even for stronger candidates, was to think that increasing the length of the tube and stem would increase sensitivity.
notes.18: A very high proportion of candidates were aware that a black surface was the better absorber, but many of these also believed that a white surface was the better emitter.
notes.20: Many candidates thought that the frequency of the wave, rather than its wavelength, would decrease when refraction occurred.
notes.25: Many candidates believed that the speed of sound in gases is greater than in metals, leading to the incorrect option A.
notes.28: The most common mistake here was to choose B, not appreciating that the current would not be rectified.
notes.30: Many weaker candidates treated this as a series, rather than parallel, arrangement, leading to option D.
notes.33: Here a very common mistake was to think that a fuse would reduce the current to its rated value.
notes.40: This question proved challenging with only the strongest candidates answering correctly. Many candidates either forgot to add on background radiation at the end of their calculation, or ignored it completely.
notes.general_comments: Many candidates found this new multiple choice paper challenging.
